items.body: The lease filed 36,646 MCF of gas and 1,405 barrels of oil, against 48,013 MCF of gas and 1,885 barrels of oil the month before. kinds.label: Production filed

kinds.label: Completions
kinds.meaning: A well finished and reported. The strongest forward signal in the record, because production usually follows within weeks.

kinds.label: Permits
kinds.meaning: Intent to drill, not a well. A feed permit carries no lease number and no location, so it is matched by county; the ones from the well map carry coordinates and are measured in miles.

kinds.label: Neighbours
kinds.meaning: What sits inside your rings, from the standing radius survey. A standing fact rather than a dated event — press 1, 3 or 5 miles to change the ring.

kinds.label: Operator changes
kinds.meaning: A lease changed hands. Worth checking the first statement from the new operator against the last from the old.

kinds.label: Well status
kinds.meaning: A well moved between producing, shut-in or plugged. How a well going quiet becomes visible before the production record catches up.

pf_blind.title: The months already produced that nobody can see yet
pf_blind.what: Texas publishes lease production two to three months after the month it happened. The newest month on the public record for your leases is June 2026, so Jul 2026, Aug 2026, Sep 2026 are produced, sold and simply not published yet.
pf_blind.means: It is the single most misread thing about a mineral statement. A month that looks empty here is far more often a month the state has not published than a month the wells did not run - and the two look identical until the filing arrives. Anything on this page covering those months is the model, which is why the chart draws them dashed.
evidence: The boundary is read off the record rather than counted back from today: a filed month carries no uncertainty band and a projected one does.

pf_depletion.title: How much of the gas is already out of the ground
pf_depletion.sub: 69% of everything this record is expected to make
pf_depletion.what: Produced to date divided by produced-plus-remaining. The first half is the state's own filings added up over the whole life of the leases; the second is the value model's remaining reserves.
pf_depletion.means: It tells you where in its life this record sits, which no monthly volume can. A decline curve front-loads badly: being well past halfway by volume happens long before the wells stop, because the tail is where most of the MONTHS are and not where most of the gas is.
evidence: 28.02M MCF filed with Texas across the whole record.
12.58M MCF still projected, to June 2032.
Oil sits at 72% by the same measure - 1.94M BBL out and 756K BBL to come.
The two are never added: a barrel and a thousand cubic feet are different things.
pf_depletion.next: Read it beside the per-lease bars under it. The portfolio figure hides the spread, and the spread is the useful part.

pf_half.title: When half of what is left arrives
pf_half.what: The projected months are walked one at a time, adding up gas, until half of everything still to come has been produced. The answer is a month the model actually carries rather than a point interpolated between two of them.
pf_half.means: This is the shape of the money, not just the volume. A curve that delivers half its remainder in the first third of its life is worth more today than one that spreads it evenly, and it is the reason a long tail on a chart is not as valuable as it looks.
evidence: 26 of the 72 projected months carry half the remaining gas.
The projection runs July 2026 to June 2032.
The curve falls 1.6% a month compounded, which is what front-loads it.
pf_half.next: If you are ever weighing an offer, this is the figure to hold next to it: most of what is left arrives sooner than the end date suggests.

pf_peak.title: The best month the state ever posted
pf_peak.what: The largest single month of gas anywhere in your filed record, and where the current rate sits against it. Both halves are the public filings; only the current rate is the model.
pf_peak.means: A monthly volume on its own tells you almost nothing - a rate is only high or low against something. Against the peak it says whether these are wells easing off a good high or wells that never had one. Being well under the peak years later is not a problem; it is what a decline curve is.

That was 2.3 years before the newest posted month.

pf_peak.next: A sharp fall against the peak that is NOT gradual is worth an email to the operator. A gradual one is the curve and needs nothing.

pf_mix.title: Which product actually pays you
pf_mix.sub: 45.7% gas, 54.3% oil of the projected money
pf_mix.what: The model carries a gas cashflow and an oil cashflow for every projected month. These are those two, added up over the whole projection and taken at your own decimal interest.
pf_mix.means: It is not the volume split and it is nowhere near it. These are gas leases - the volume is overwhelmingly gas - but a barrel sells for roughly thirty times what a thousand cubic feet does, so the liquid carries far more of the money than of the production. Which means your income moves with the oil price more than the volumes would ever suggest.
evidence: Gas and oil cashflow add exactly to the total on every row of the model, so these two shares always come to a hundred.
The wells make about 69.2 BBL of oil for every thousand MCF of gas.
There is no honest single percentage for "how much of the volume is gas": the two are different units, and adding them is the blended figure this app refuses to show.
pf_mix.next: When you read a price headline, the oil one moves your statement more than the gas one does on this record - the opposite of what the volumes imply.

pf_deck.title: The price path every figure here is built on
pf_deck.what: The forward price the value model was run on, month by month. It is the model's own deck and not the settlements in the ticker at the top of the screen, which are today's published market.
pf_deck.means: Every dollar figure on this page rides on it, and it is the single biggest reason the estimate changes between runs - more than the volumes do. A deck that assumes a falling oil price is why the later years look thinner than the decline rate alone would make them.

pf_deck.next: Compare it with the live settlements in the ticker. Where the deck is below the market, the estimate is the conservative one.

It holds prices at the model's deck, it cannot see the gathering and compression deducts your operator applies, and it assumes the wells behave the way the curve says. pf_removed.title: The gas that never reaches the sales meter
pf_removed.what: Texas splits each month between disposition codes and records separately the volume that left the stream before the sales meter. A royalty is calculated on what reached the meter, so the smaller of those two figures is the one that turns into money.
pf_removed.means: This is the gap between "what my wells produced" and "what I was paid on", and it is normally invisible. On your record it is not one number: it follows the route the gas leaves under, and your leases do not all use the same route.

pf_removed.next: Your statement should show a volume close to the metered figure rather than the posted one. If it is materially below even that, the difference is deducts and worth asking about.

pf_decline.title: How fast the curve falls
pf_decline.sub: 1.6% a month, compounded across the projection
pf_decline.what: The constant month-on-month rate that would carry the first projected month down to the last. It is the compounded rate and not the average of the steps, which overstates it, nor the first step, which reports whatever happened to be noisy about one month.
pf_decline.means: Read it as a shape rather than a schedule. A decline curve flattens as it falls, so the early years of a projection are much larger than the late ones and the final years are thin and very long. The rate differs lease by lease, and the spread is usually more interesting than the average.

The curve flattens as it falls, so the real tail is longer and thinner than this number - the figure tells you how much is left relative to the current rate, not the date the wells stop. It is also the figure that moves most when a neighbour completes a good well and your operator reworks yours.

pf_oil.title: The oil these gas leases make
pf_oil.what: The liquid that comes up with the gas and drops out at the surface. It is metered separately from the gas, filed in its own column, and sells against the oil benchmark. Texas classifies every lease on this record as a gas lease.
pf_oil.means: It is a much bigger part of your income than of your production. Oil is 54.3% of the projected money while the wells make about 69.2 BBL for every thousand MCF of gas - because a barrel sells for roughly thirty times what a thousand cubic feet does.
